stem: A 55-year-old patient with known cirrhosis vomits approximately 700 mL of fresh blood. He is pale, BP 86/50 mmHg, pulse 128/min and remains alert. Large-bore IV access is available.
ask: Which ONE management bundle is MOST APPROPRIATE while arranging urgent endoscopy?
options: High-dose oral proton-pump inhibitor alone
Resuscitation, IV vasoactive therapy for varices and prophylactic antibiotics
Immediate discharge after a single normal haemoglobin reading
Thrombolysis and antiplatelet loading
Nasogastric lavage as the only stabilisation step
explanations: A PPI alone does not treat portal-hypertensive bleeding or shock.
Probable variceal bleeding needs ABC resuscitation, blood products as indicated, early vasoactive medication such as terlipressin or octreotide, antibiotics, and endoscopic control.
Haemoglobin can initially appear normal during major acute blood loss.
Antithrombotics worsen active haemorrhage.
Gastric lavage is not definitive resuscitation or haemostasis.
pearl: Treat suspected variceal bleeding before endoscopy confirms the source; antibiotics improve outcomes.
pivot: If bleeding is proven non-variceal peptic ulcer disease, endoscopic therapy and acid suppression become central rather than a variceal bundle.

stem: A 37-year-old woman has frothy urine, leg oedema and serum albumin 21 g/L. Urine protein-to-creatinine ratio is markedly elevated. Urine microscopy shows fatty casts but no red cell casts.
ask: Which ONE syndrome BEST explains the findings?
options: Nephritic syndrome due to acute glomerulonephritis
Acute pyelonephritis
Distal renal tubular acidosis
Isolated pre-renal azotaemia
Nephrotic syndrome
explanations: Nephritic syndrome usually centres on haematuria, red cell casts and often hypertension or renal impairment.
Pyelonephritis presents with fever, flank pain and pyuria.
RTA is characterised by acid-base disturbance, not massive proteinuria.
Pre-renal azotaemia does not explain fatty casts and heavy proteinuria.
Heavy protein loss causes hypoalbuminaemia, oedema and lipiduria, the classic nephrotic pattern.
pearl: Nephrotic syndrome increases thrombosis risk because anticoagulant proteins can be lost in urine.
pivot: If dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts predominate, consider nephritic glomerular inflammation.

stem: A 43-year-old patient develops widespread urticaria, wheeze and BP 76/40 mmHg within minutes of receiving an IV antibiotic. A nurse has stopped the infusion.
ask: Which ONE drug and route is MOST APPROPRIATE FIRST?
options: Administer IV adrenaline as a rapid undiluted bolus in a conscious patient
Give nebulised salbutamol before any adrenaline
Intramuscular adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh
Start rapid IV crystalloid only and reassess in ten minutes
Give IV antihistamine plus corticosteroid without adrenaline
explanations: An undiluted IV bolus risks severe dysrhythmia; standard first-line is IM adrenaline outside specialised arrest settings.
Salbutamol is adjunctive for bronchospasm and does not reverse shock or laryngeal oedema.
IM adrenaline is the first-line lifesaving therapy for anaphylaxis, addressing airway swelling, bronchospasm and shock; repeat as required and resuscitate.
Fluids support circulation but cannot replace adrenaline for anaphylaxis.
Antihistamines and steroids do not reverse life-threatening airway and circulatory compromise quickly.
pearl: Anaphylaxis is a clinical diagnosis: do not wait for tryptase before giving adrenaline.
pivot: Isolated hives with stable breathing and blood pressure may be managed without adrenaline, with monitoring and clinical assessment.

stem: A 5-year-old with nephrotic syndrome has increasing facial and leg oedema. Serum albumin is 15 g/L, urine has 4+ protein and BP is normal. He becomes suddenly breathless with pleuritic chest pain.
ask: Which ONE complication should be HIGH on the differential?
options: Isolated viral conjunctivitis
Acute otitis media
Pulmonary thromboembolism due to nephrotic hypercoagulability
Simple iron deficiency alone
Functional abdominal pain
explanations: Conjunctivitis does not cause pleuritic dyspnoea.
Otitis media is unrelated to sudden chest symptoms.
Nephrotic syndrome causes a prothrombotic state from loss of anticoagulant proteins, so sudden pleuritic dyspnoea warrants PE assessment.
Anaemia may cause exertional dyspnoea but typically not abrupt pleuritic pain.
Functional pain does not explain an acute respiratory event.
pearl: Nephrotic syndrome is not just oedema: consider thrombosis and serious infection.
pivot: If fever and abdominal tenderness predominate, also consider spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.

stem: A 7-year-old has five days of fever, bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue, diffuse rash and unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy. ECG is normal and he is haemodynamically stable.
ask: Which ONE complication drives urgent specialist treatment?
options: Permanent isolated conductive hearing loss
Congenital hip dysplasia
Coronary artery aneurysm formation
Chronic liver cirrhosis
Ruptured appendix
explanations: Hearing loss is not the signature life-threatening complication.
Hip dysplasia is unrelated.
Kawasaki disease is systemic vasculitis involving medium arteries; coronary aneurysm risk is reduced with timely immunoglobulin-based treatment.
Cirrhosis is not the expected major outcome.
Appendiceal rupture is a different surgical disease.
pearl: Five days of fever plus mucocutaneous signs suggest Kawasaki disease; assess the heart even if the initial ECG is normal.
pivot: If a child is in shock with high inflammatory markers and recent SARS-CoV-2, consider MIS-C and its overlapping presentation.

stem: A 66-year-old woman wakes with right facial weakness, arm weakness and expressive aphasia. The right forehead moves normally. She has no limb ataxia.
ask: Which ONE lesion localisation is MOST CONSISTENT?
options: Right peripheral facial nerve lesion
Left cerebral hemisphere involving a dominant middle cerebral artery territory
Right cerebellar hemisphere lesion
Left peripheral facial nerve lesion
Isolated cervical spinal cord lesion
explanations: A peripheral VII lesion causes ipsilateral whole-face weakness and cannot explain aphasia.
Contralateral face/arm weakness with forehead sparing and aphasia implies a dominant left supratentorial cortical lesion, commonly MCA territory.
A cerebellar lesion tends to cause ataxia rather than aphasia with arm weakness.
Peripheral left facial palsy affects the left whole face and not the arm.
Cervical cord lesions do not cause aphasia or facial weakness.
pearl: Forehead sparing suggests an upper motor neuron facial pattern; aphasia implies dominant cortical involvement.
pivot: If both forehead and lower face are weak ipsilaterally without arm signs, consider peripheral Bell palsy after excluding red flags.

stem: A 21-year-old man with severe asthma is exhausted after repeated bronchodilator therapy. His respiratory rate has fallen from 38/min to 15/min, he speaks only single words, and his chest is almost silent. Oxygen saturation is 91% despite supplemental oxygen.
ask: Which ONE interpretation is MOST APPROPRIATE?
options: Clinical improvement because tachypnoea has resolved
Give additional bronchodilator doses but defer senior review until peak flow can be measured
Start a sedative to reduce work of breathing
Arrange a routine ward review after the next nebuliser
Impending respiratory failure requiring immediate senior airway support
explanations: Falling respiratory rate with exhaustion and silent chest can indicate respiratory muscle failure.
Bronchodilators should continue, but delaying resuscitation/airway planning is unsafe.
Sedation can suppress ventilation and accelerate arrest.
This is a life-threatening exacerbation needing urgent escalation, not routine assessment.
In a tiring asthmatic patient, decreasing respiratory effort and a silent chest reflect critically poor airflow, not recovery.
pearl: A silent chest, drowsiness, exhaustion or rising PaCO₂ are ominous in asthma.
pivot: A patient who is talking comfortably with improving air entry and decreasing work of breathing may truly be responding.

stem: A 32-year-old G1P0 at 36 weeks has pruritus, especially on palms and soles, worse at night. There is no rash. Serum bile acids are raised and transaminases mildly elevated.
ask: Which ONE fetal complication is MOST ASSOCIATED with this condition?
options: Congenital neural tube defects due to folate deficiency
Fetal hydrops caused by Rh incompatibility
Placental accreta spectrum
Meconium ileus from cystic fibrosis
Increased risk of stillbirth, particularly with markedly elevated bile acids
explanations: Neural tube defects are developmental anomalies, not a consequence of maternal cholestasis.
Rh alloimmunisation causes immune fetal anaemia; no evidence here.
Placenta accreta relates to abnormal placentation, often with prior uterine surgery.
Meconium ileus is associated with CF rather than maternal bile acids.
Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy is associated with adverse fetal outcomes, especially at higher bile acid concentrations, informing monitoring and planned birth.
pearl: Pruritus of palms/soles without rash in pregnancy should trigger bile acid testing.
pivot: If prominent rash with normal bile acids appears, investigate dermatologic pregnancy conditions instead.

stem: A 45-year-old man with CKD is prescribed trimethoprim for urinary symptoms while continuing lisinopril and spironolactone. Three days later, his potassium is 6.5 mmol/L and ECG shows peaked T waves.
ask: Which ONE medication-related mechanism MOST plausibly contributed?
options: Excessive urinary potassium losses caused by trimethoprim
Additive impairment of renal potassium excretion
Renal potassium wasting from spironolactone
An isolated increase in dietary potassium absorption from lisinopril
Reduced gastrointestinal absorption of sodium
explanations: Trimethoprim more commonly promotes retention than loss of potassium.
Trimethoprim can act like an epithelial sodium channel blocker; combining it with ACE inhibitors and potassium-sparing diuretics raises hyperkalaemia risk, especially in CKD.
Spironolactone is potassium-sparing, not potassium-wasting.
ACE inhibition primarily lowers aldosterone-mediated renal excretion, not dietary absorption.
Altered sodium absorption does not explain this characteristic drug interaction.
pearl: Reconcile interacting medications and renal function when prescribing antibiotics in CKD.
pivot: If the patient were hypokalaemic on loop diuretics instead, renal potassium wasting would be a different diagnostic direction.

stem: A 64-year-old patient with metastatic cancer has clearly documented a valid refusal of blood transfusion while competent. Now unconscious, she develops severe anaemia. There is no new information suggesting the directive was revoked.
ask: Which ONE ethical principle is MOST RELEVANT when considering her prior decision?
options: Respect for the patient’s previously expressed informed refusal, subject to applicable law
The treating team may always override a competent refusal if survival is at stake
A family member automatically supersedes any prior valid directive
Unconsciousness permanently nullifies all previous treatment decisions
Only the clinician’s personal values determine treatment
explanations: Advance refusals and prior competent choices merit respect according to jurisdictional legal requirements and validity/applicability to the current situation.
Beneficence does not erase a competent patient’s informed refusal.
Family input helps establish wishes but does not automatically override a valid decision.
Loss of consciousness does not retroactively remove prior autonomy.
Clinical ethics does not grant clinicians unilateral value-based authority.
pearl: Capacity is assessed for the relevant decision at the time; document informed refusals clearly and follow local law.
pivot: If the validity or applicability of the directive is genuinely uncertain, seek urgent senior and legal/ethics input while stabilising what can safely be done.

stem: A 58-year-old man has ptosis and diplopia worsening through the day, difficulty swallowing and now weak cough. His oxygen saturation remains 97% on room air but forced vital capacity is falling.
ask: Which ONE is the MOST APPROPRIATE immediate priority?
options: Escalate for impending myasthenic respiratory crisis with close ventilatory monitoring and airway planning
Reassure because pulse oximetry is normal
Begin heavy exercise to build respiratory strength
Give a sedating benzodiazepine before any assessment
Discharge with a routine ophthalmology appointment
explanations: Bulbar weakness and falling FVC indicate impending ventilatory failure in myasthenia even before oxygen desaturation.
Saturation may stay normal until late in hypoventilation.
Exercise can worsen fatigable weakness during crisis.
Sedatives may compromise airway/ventilation.
This is an acute life-threatening neuromuscular presentation.
pearl: In neuromuscular failure, serial FVC and bulbar examination can be more useful than SpO₂ alone.
pivot: With isolated stable ocular myasthenia and no bulbar/respiratory signs, routine outpatient therapy may be appropriate.

stem: A term baby has transposition of the great arteries with profound cyanosis despite oxygen. Echocardiography shows a restrictive interatrial communication and a closing ductus arteriosus.
ask: Which ONE emergency intervention directly improves intracardiac mixing if prostaglandin is insufficient?
options: Indomethacin to close the ductus
Balloon atrial septostomy
Elective closure of the atrial communication
Oral propranolol as definitive therapy
Pulmonary valve balloon dilation
explanations: Duct closure can further reduce mixing; prostaglandin maintains patency.
TGA requires mixing between parallel circulations; balloon atrial septostomy enlarges an inadequate atrial communication and can rapidly improve oxygen delivery.
Closing the atrial communication worsens systemic oxygenation.
Propranolol does not create circulatory mixing.
Pulmonary valvuloplasty does not correct atrial restriction in TGA.
pearl: Critical cyanotic heart disease may need prostaglandin, urgent echo and catheter intervention, not simply more oxygen.
pivot: When atrial mixing is already adequate, prostaglandin and early arterial switch planning may be sufficient initial measures.

stem: A 60-year-old woman with a new painless palpable breast lump has a suspicious irregular solid lesion on ultrasound. The axilla is clinically normal.
ask: Which ONE is the MOST APPROPRIATE next diagnostic step?
options: Order contrast-enhanced breast MRI instead of sampling the suspicious ultrasound lesion
Image-guided core needle biopsy of the lesion
Perform fine-needle aspiration alone as the definitive histological assessment
Start empirical endocrine therapy without histological confirmation
Repeat imaging at six months despite suspicious malignant features
explanations: MRI may be helpful in selected staging/problem-solving settings but cannot replace tissue diagnosis here.
Core biopsy provides tissue architecture for malignancy diagnosis and receptor testing, following appropriate triple assessment.
FNA does not consistently provide tumour architecture and receptor profiling required for planning.
Endocrine therapy requires diagnosis and receptor results.
A suspicious mass should not be deferred to routine surveillance.
pearl: Triple assessment of a breast lesion: clinical assessment, appropriate imaging and tissue sampling.
pivot: For a simple clearly benign cyst, ultrasound-guided aspiration may serve a different diagnostic or therapeutic role.

stem: A 6-year-old has palpable purpura on both legs, arthralgia and abdominal pain after an upper respiratory infection. Platelets are normal. Urinalysis shows blood and protein.
ask: Which ONE additional assessment is MOST IMPORTANT to monitor over time?
options: Serial serum amylase only
Daily peak expiratory flow without respiratory symptoms
Blood pressure and renal function/urinalysis
Repeated serum troponin without cardiac symptoms
Routine visual acuity only
explanations: Amylase does not track the major long-term complication.
Respiratory obstruction is not the hallmark concern.
IgA vasculitis can cause delayed nephritis even when initial symptoms improve, making blood pressure and urine/renal follow-up essential.
Myocardial injury is not a routine surveillance target.
Vision alone misses renal disease.
pearl: The important long-term threat in IgA vasculitis is renal involvement.
pivot: If severe abdominal pain with GI bleeding occurs, assess for bowel complications including intussusception.

stem: A 24-year-old woman has sharp pleuritic chest pain that improves when leaning forward. An ECG shows diffuse concave ST elevation and PR depression. Troponin is mildly raised; bedside echocardiography shows no large effusion.
ask: Which ONE diagnosis BEST unifies these findings?
options: Acute anterior STEMI from an LAD occlusion
Pulmonary embolism
Acute myopericarditis
Aortic dissection
Benign early repolarisation without inflammation
explanations: A territorial STEMI usually has regional changes and reciprocal depression.
PE may cause chest pain and troponin rise but not classic diffuse PR depression.
Positional pleuritic pain with diffuse ST elevation and PR depression supports pericardial inflammation; raised troponin suggests accompanying myocardial involvement.
Dissection causes abrupt tearing pain and is not described by this ECG pattern.
Early repolarisation lacks the inflammatory syndrome and troponin rise.
pearl: Pericarditis often produces diffuse rather than coronary-territory ST elevation; raised troponin indicates possible myocardial involvement.
pivot: If focal ST elevation with reciprocal changes and crushing pain predominates, urgently exclude coronary occlusion.

stem: A 10-year-old with type 1 diabetes presents with vomiting, ketones 5.5 mmol/L, pH 7.17 and glucose 24 mmol/L. Three hours into DKA treatment he develops headache, bradycardia and reduced consciousness.
ask: Which ONE complication must be treated as an emergency?
options: Cerebral injury/raised intracranial pressure during DKA management
Expected harmless headache from dehydration
Isolated mild hypophosphataemia
Chronic diabetic neuropathy
Simple motion sickness
explanations: Worsening consciousness, headache and bradycardia during paediatric DKA raise concern for cerebral injury; urgent critical care assessment and hyperosmolar therapy may be needed.
The neurological trajectory is a danger sign, not a routine symptom.
Phosphate loss does not typically cause this acute Cushing-like presentation.
Neuropathy is a chronic complication.
Motion sickness cannot explain reduced consciousness with bradycardia.
pearl: New neurological signs during paediatric DKA demand immediate escalation; do not wait for confirmatory imaging to act.
pivot: If neurological status steadily improves with correction, continue careful protocol-driven monitoring.

stem: A 59-year-old man has progressive dyspnoea and dry cough over 18 months. On examination, there are fine late-inspiratory bibasal crackles and finger clubbing. Spirometry shows reduced TLC and FVC with a normal-to-high FEV1/FVC ratio.
ask: Which ONE is the MOST LIKELY pulmonary process?
options: Uncomplicated COPD with predominant emphysema
Acute bronchial asthma
Fibrotic interstitial lung disease
Vocal cord dysfunction
An isolated large airway foreign body
explanations: Emphysema generally produces an obstructive FEV1/FVC and often hyperinflation.
Asthma has episodic variable airflow obstruction and usually no clubbing.
The chronic progressive course, clubbing, fine crackles and restriction indicate fibrotic interstitial disease rather than airway obstruction.
Vocal cord dysfunction typically causes episodic upper-airway symptoms.
Foreign-body obstruction is not a typical progressive bilateral restrictive syndrome.
pearl: Restrictive spirometry requires confirmation with lung volumes; high-resolution CT characterises interstitial patterns.
pivot: If spirometry instead shows reduced FEV1/FVC with bronchodilator reversibility, asthma becomes more likely.

stem: A 64-year-old man is day 5 after a colorectal anastomosis. He develops persistent tachycardia (120/min), new abdominal pain, fever and oliguria. His wound is clean. Lactate is 3.9 mmol/L.
ask: Which ONE is the MOST IMPORTANT working diagnosis to urgently exclude?
options: Normal postoperative inflammatory pain
Minor superficial wound cellulitis
Uncomplicated postoperative constipation
An isolated drug-related rash
Anastomotic leak causing intra-abdominal sepsis
explanations: Normal pain should not cause this evolving shock picture.
A clean wound and deep systemic illness argue against isolated superficial cellulitis.
Constipation is not a sufficient explanation for rising lactate and oliguria.
Rash does not explain acute abdominal pain with organ hypoperfusion.
New sepsis physiology on day 5 after bowel anastomosis is an anastomotic leak until safely excluded, requiring resuscitation, antibiotics, imaging as appropriate and urgent surgical escalation.
pearl: Unexplained postoperative tachycardia may be the earliest warning of anastomotic leakage.
pivot: If the patient has diffuse peritonitis or is unstable, source-control decisions may supersede waiting for CT.

stem: A 61-year-old man has recurrent renal stones, bone pain and constipation. Calcium is 3.05 mmol/L, phosphate is low and parathyroid hormone is inappropriately elevated.
ask: Which ONE endocrine disorder is MOST LIKELY?
options: Malignancy-associated hypercalcaemia mediated solely by PTHrP
Primary hyperparathyroidism
Vitamin D deficiency with uncomplicated secondary hyperparathyroidism
Hypoparathyroidism
Severe hypomagnesaemia causing low PTH
explanations: PTHrP typically suppresses endogenous PTH.
Hypercalcaemia with non-suppressed or elevated PTH is PTH-dependent, classically primary hyperparathyroidism.
Secondary hyperparathyroidism from vitamin D deficiency usually has low/normal calcium.
Hypoparathyroidism causes low PTH and hypocalcaemia.
Severe hypomagnesaemia can suppress PTH, not produce classic PTH-dependent hypercalcaemia.
pearl: When assessing hypercalcaemia, ask whether PTH is appropriately suppressed.
pivot: If PTH is low, consider malignancy, excess vitamin D and other PTH-independent causes.

stem: A 30-year-old woman is 20 minutes postpartum after a vaginal birth. She is bleeding heavily; the uterus is large and boggy. Placenta appears complete and there is no obvious genital tract tear. She is tachycardic.
ask: Which ONE is the MOST APPROPRIATE first targeted measure for the likely cause?
options: Immediate methotrexate
Long-term oral iron as sole treatment
Uterine massage and prompt uterotonic treatment while activating postpartum haemorrhage resuscitation
Abdominal CT before any resuscitation
Wait for blood group testing before stimulating the uterus
explanations: Methotrexate treats select trophoblastic/ectopic indications, not uterine atony.
Iron replaces stores later but does not stop acute bleeding.
An atonic uterus is the commonest postpartum haemorrhage cause; massage, oxytocin and haemorrhage protocols start immediately.
Imaging should not delay haemorrhage control.
Resuscitation and uterotonics must begin while labs and crossmatch are obtained.
pearl: Think 4 Ts of PPH: Tone, Trauma, Tissue, Thrombin.
pivot: If uterus is firm with ongoing heavy bleeding, examine for trauma, retained tissue and coagulopathy.

stem: A 69-year-old woman with previous abdominal surgery has cramping abdominal pain, vomiting and distension. CT shows dilated small-bowel loops and a transition point. After observation she develops constant severe pain, fever, tachycardia and rising lactate.
ask: Which ONE complication is MOST CONCERNING?
options: Strangulation with bowel ischaemia
Uncomplicated adhesional obstruction resolving spontaneously
Functional constipation alone
Mild viral gastroenteritis
Chronic irritable bowel syndrome
explanations: Conversion from colicky to constant pain with systemic toxicity and hyperlactataemia suggests compromised perfusion and potential necrosis: urgent surgery review is needed.
Uncomplicated obstruction lacks signs of evolving systemic toxicity.
Constipation does not explain a transition point plus shock features.
Gastroenteritis more often causes diarrhoea and no mechanical transition.
IBS does not cause lactic acidosis and severe obstruction.
pearl: Constant pain, peritonism, fever, tachycardia and acidosis are danger signs in bowel obstruction.
pivot: If stable without peritonism or ischaemic signs, selected adhesional obstructions can undergo a supervised nonoperative trial.

stem: A 66-year-old man taking warfarin for atrial fibrillation fell and struck his head. He now has a severe headache but is fully oriented and has no focal neurological deficit. His INR is 3.5.
ask: Which ONE is the MOST APPROPRIATE next investigation?
options: Observe for six hours and scan only if a deficit develops
Order MRI brain with contrast as the first acute test
Reverse warfarin immediately in every head injury before imaging irrespective of clinical findings
Urgent non-contrast CT brain
Repeat the INR tomorrow and decide about CT at that point
explanations: Intracranial bleeding may precede focal signs; observation alone misses an important diagnosis.
CT is usually faster and the initial test for acute traumatic blood.
Reversal decisions depend on bleeding, clinical urgency and protocol; imaging and assessment should not be replaced by indiscriminate reversal.
Anticoagulation after head injury increases intracranial haemorrhage risk; prompt non-contrast CT is needed despite an initially reassuring examination.
The immediate question is whether an intracranial bleed is present, not whether INR has changed by tomorrow.
pearl: In anticoagulated head trauma, absence of focal signs does not reliably exclude bleeding.
pivot: If haemorrhage is found, urgent reversal of anticoagulation and neurosurgical assessment may be needed.

stem: A 74-year-old woman presents with a new unilateral headache, scalp tenderness and jaw pain on chewing. She reports transient loss of vision in one eye. Examination shows reduced temporal artery pulsation.
ask: Which ONE action is MOST APPROPRIATE to prevent irreversible visual loss?
options: Wait for temporal artery biopsy before giving any treatment
Treat only with a short course of antibiotics
Reassure that transient monocular blindness is benign
Prescribe triptan and avoid any further work-up
Start high-dose glucocorticoid treatment urgently while arranging confirmatory assessment
explanations: Biopsy or vascular imaging can follow; treatment should not wait.
Antibiotics do not treat granulomatous arterial inflammation.
Amaurosis fugax is a medical emergency in this context.
A presumed migraine diagnosis risks blindness.
Giant cell arteritis threatens permanent visual loss; strong clinical suspicion with visual symptoms warrants immediate glucocorticoids and urgent specialist care.
pearl: GCA is most common after age 50; jaw claudication and visual symptoms are particularly concerning clues.
pivot: If a younger patient has similar transient monocular visual loss, investigate other urgent vascular or ocular causes instead of assuming GCA.

stem: A 24-year-old woman with heavy menstrual bleeding has Hb 82 g/L, MCV 67 fL, low ferritin and high total iron-binding capacity. A peripheral film shows microcytosis and hypochromia.
ask: Which ONE diagnosis is MOST CONSISTENT?
options: Anaemia of chronic inflammation with iron sequestration
Thalassaemia trait
Iron deficiency anaemia
Sideroblastic anaemia
Mixed vitamin B12 and folate deficiency
explanations: Inflammation often has high ferritin and low TIBC rather than both low ferritin and high TIBC.
Thalassaemia is microcytic, but ferritin is not typically low and RBC count may be relatively preserved.
Microcytic hypochromic anaemia with depleted ferritin and increased iron-binding capacity supports iron deficiency, likely from menstrual loss.
Sideroblastic conditions tend to have impaired utilisation with normal/high stores.
Megaloblastic deficiencies favour macrocytosis and lack classic iron-depletion indices.
pearl: Always investigate the cause of iron deficiency, including menstrual and gastrointestinal blood loss where appropriate.
pivot: If the MCV is disproportionately low with a relatively high RBC count and normal ferritin, consider thalassaemia trait.

stem: A 53-year-old man has haemoptysis, haematuria and rapidly rising creatinine. Chest imaging shows bilateral alveolar infiltrates. Urine microscopy contains dysmorphic RBCs and red cell casts.
ask: Which ONE mechanism BEST unifies the pulmonary and renal findings?
options: Pulmonary embolism with coincidental microscopic haematuria
Pulmonary–renal small-vessel immune injury such as anti-GBM disease or ANCA vasculitis
Community-acquired pneumonia with simple cystitis
Decompensated heart failure causing cardiorenal syndrome
Isolated chronic diabetic nephropathy and bronchitis
explanations: PE can cause haemoptysis but does not explain RBC casts with rapidly progressive glomerular AKI.
Alveolar haemorrhage together with glomerular bleeding and AKI is a pulmonary–renal syndrome requiring urgent nephrology/respiratory assessment.
Cystitis causes nonglomerular haematuria and does not produce RBC casts.
Heart failure can cause infiltrates and kidney dysfunction but not active glomerular red-cell casts.
This would be an unlikely coincidence for abrupt alveolar haemorrhage and glomerulonephritis.
pearl: Red cell casts are a strong clue to glomerular inflammation; combine with pulmonary symptoms to identify emergencies.
pivot: Anti-GBM serology, ANCA testing and renal biopsy may guide targeted therapy, but stabilisation and urgent specialist treatment are time-critical.

stem: A 73-year-old patient develops left lower abdominal pain and fever. CT shows sigmoid diverticulitis with a 5.5-cm pericolic abscess but no free intraperitoneal air. She is haemodynamically stable.
ask: Which ONE strategy is MOST APPROPRIATE?
options: IV antibiotics plus assessment for image-guided percutaneous drainage
Discharge with dietary advice alone
Immediate total colectomy for every diverticular abscess
Give laxatives and defer treatment for a week
Treat with oral antacids alone
explanations: A sizeable contained diverticular abscess commonly requires antibiotics and consideration of percutaneous drainage, guided by accessibility and local expertise.
A large abscess warrants inpatient assessment and source-control planning.
Surgery is indicated in selected cases but not automatically for a stable contained abscess.
Delaying sepsis management risks deterioration.
Antacids do not treat diverticular infection.
pearl: In complicated diverticulitis, abscess size, access, sepsis and peritonitis determine antibiotics versus drainage versus surgery.
pivot: Generalised peritonitis, haemodynamic instability or failed source control can necessitate urgent operative management.

stem: An inpatient with a documented penicillin anaphylaxis is prescribed intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam for sepsis. You are the junior doctor asked to administer the first dose; the patient is currently haemodynamically stable.
ask: Which ONE action is MOST APPROPRIATE?
options: Withhold the ordered drug and urgently clarify a safe antibiotic plan with the senior team
Administer a test dose without supervision
Delete the allergy entry because the patient cannot remember the brand
Delay all antibiotics until the next ward round
Give the drug after administering prophylactic antihistamine
explanations: A history of genuine immediate beta-lactam anaphylaxis requires urgent review of antibiotic selection, balancing timely sepsis therapy against allergy risk.
An unsupervised test dose may trigger severe anaphylaxis.
Uncertainty about a drug name does not justify erasing a documented severe reaction.
Sepsis still requires prompt alternative effective therapy.
Antihistamines do not prevent anaphylactic shock.
pearl: Before administration: check drug, dose, route, patient, indication, renal function and serious allergies.
pivot: If the allergy history is uncertain rather than documented anaphylaxis, rapid structured assessment may permit an appropriate beta-lactam under local policy.

stem: A 30-year-old man has had 18 hours of vomiting and abdominal pain. His glucose is 29 mmol/L, blood ketones 6.1 mmol/L, pH 7.11, and potassium 2.8 mmol/L. He is alert, with no ECG arrhythmia, and intravenous fluids have commenced.
ask: Which ONE is the MOST APPROPRIATE action BEFORE starting an insulin infusion?
options: Start the usual insulin infusion while replacing potassium concurrently
Give sodium bicarbonate first because pH is below 7.2
Replace potassium urgently with ECG and electrolyte monitoring
Administer potassium only after blood glucose falls below 15 mmol/L
Delay potassium treatment while confirming the result on a second sample
explanations: At K 2.8 mmol/L, insulin can drive potassium even lower, so replacement must precede infusion.
Bicarbonate is not routinely indicated at pH 7.11 and may exacerbate hypokalaemia.
Insulin drives potassium into cells, so starting it with marked hypokalaemia risks lethal arrhythmia; correct K⁺ first while continuing resuscitation.
The potassium deficit is dangerous now, independent of glucose trajectory.
Prompt confirmation may be reasonable if spurious, but do not delay correction of clearly severe hypokalaemia with consistent clinical context.
pearl: DKA has total-body potassium depletion even when the initial serum potassium is normal or high.
pivot: If potassium were 5.5 mmol/L, insulin could usually begin with close serial potassium monitoring and no initial K⁺ supplementation.

stem: A 72-year-old patient taking antibiotics for a respiratory infection develops watery diarrhoea eight times daily, abdominal cramping and fever. WBC is 21 × 10⁹/L and creatinine has doubled.
ask: Which ONE cause should be assessed urgently?
options: Clostridioides difficile colitis
Lactose intolerance alone
Uncomplicated irritable bowel syndrome
Functional constipation
A harmless expected side effect with no investigation
explanations: Antibiotic exposure followed by significant diarrhoea and systemic inflammatory/renal features suggests potentially severe C. difficile infection.
Lactose intolerance does not explain marked leukocytosis and acute kidney injury.
IBS does not cause fever or substantial inflammatory response.
Constipation is opposite the dominant symptom.
Severe diarrhoea plus organ injury is not a benign medication nuisance.
pearl: Test appropriately only in patients with clinically significant unformed stools; assess severity and isolation needs.
pivot: If the patient develops shock, ileus or toxic megacolon, escalate for fulminant infection and surgical input.

stem: A 39-year-old woman has a painful irreducible groin swelling, repeated vomiting and abdominal distension. There is overlying tenderness and mild tachycardia.
ask: Which ONE is the MOST APPROPRIATE management priority?
options: Attempt forceful reduction despite bowel-obstruction features
Order outpatient elective repair after bowel symptoms resolve
Give analgesia and observe overnight without surgical involvement
Perform a routine ultrasound and defer action until its report is available
Urgent surgical assessment for incarcerated or strangulated hernia
explanations: Forceful taxis may reduce ischaemic bowel into the abdomen and delay recognition.
Pain, irreducibility and vomiting indicate an emergency rather than uncomplicated elective hernia.
Analgesia is important but not definitive evaluation for bowel compromise.
Imaging can help when uncertain but must not delay surgical assessment of an obstructed hernia.
An irreducible painful hernia with obstruction threatens bowel viability and requires urgent surgical evaluation.
pearl: Femoral hernias have a comparatively high risk of strangulation, especially in women.
pivot: A soft, painless, reducible hernia without obstructive symptoms may be suitable for planned elective assessment.

stem: A 19-year-old woman has abrupt severe unilateral pelvic pain after exercise and repeated vomiting. She has a 7-cm ovarian cyst. Doppler ultrasound demonstrates some arterial flow to the ovary.
ask: Which ONE statement is MOST APPROPRIATE?
options: Presence of Doppler arterial flow reliably excludes torsion
Repeat pelvic ultrasound in 48 hours before gynaecology review
Treat as a simple ruptured cyst because vomiting confirms rupture
Ovarian torsion remains a concern despite detectable Doppler flow
Order serum CA-125 to determine whether urgent surgery is indicated
explanations: The ovary has dual arterial supply; torsion may retain detectable flow.
Delayed assessment risks ovarian infarction in high-suspicion presentations.
Rupture is an alternative, but abrupt pain plus mass and vomiting warrants urgent torsion assessment.
Dual ovarian blood supply means flow may be present in torsion; clinical suspicion requires urgent gynaecology evaluation for laparoscopy.
Tumour markers do not diagnose or exclude acute torsion.
pearl: For torsion, clinical history can outweigh a reassuring ultrasound Doppler report.
pivot: If pain is gradual and a cyst is simple without torsion features, management may be different after full assessment.

stem: A 40-year-old man with schizophrenia has been stable on clozapine for six months. He now has four days of constipation, distension, abdominal pain and vomiting. Bowel sounds are reduced.
ask: Which ONE action is MOST APPROPRIATE?
options: Simply increase clozapine to treat somatic preoccupation
Reassure that constipation is always harmless on clozapine
Treat with a bulk-forming fibre agent alone despite possible obstruction
Wait for the next routine blood count before acting
Urgent medical/surgical assessment for clozapine-induced gastrointestinal hypomotility
explanations: Higher clozapine exposure can worsen hypomotility.
Clozapine constipation can become fatal.
Bulk-forming agents may be inappropriate in severe hypomotility or obstruction.
Neutrophil monitoring does not replace acute bowel assessment.
Clozapine can cause severe hypomotility, ileus and fatal bowel obstruction; vomiting and distension are emergency features.
pearl: For clozapine, monitor bowel function proactively and escalate red flags such as pain, distension and vomiting.
pivot: With mild constipation and no alarm features, a structured bowel regimen can be managed under protocol.

stem: A 35-year-old man suffers a closed tibial fracture after a motorcycle crash. Despite analgesia he has escalating pain with passive toe stretch, a tense calf and paresthesia. Distal pulses remain palpable.
ask: Which ONE is the MOST APPROPRIATE response?
options: Reassure because palpable pulses exclude compartment syndrome
Apply a tight circumferential cast immediately
Wait until permanent paralysis occurs before acting
Raise the leg well above heart level as the only measure
Urgent orthopaedic evaluation for acute compartment syndrome and fasciotomy
explanations: Palpable pulses do not rule out raised compartment pressure.
Tight casting may worsen pressure.
Paralysis is a late irreversible finding.
Excessive elevation may lower perfusion pressure and does not decompress fascia.
Disproportionate pain, passive stretch pain and tense compartments suggest limb-threatening compartment syndrome; pulses may remain present until late.
pearl: Pain on passive stretch is an early clue; compartment syndrome is primarily a clinical emergency.
pivot: If examination is unreliable, serial assessment and compartment pressure measurement may aid decision-making, without delaying treatment when clear.

stem: A 52-year-old man has a painless swollen left testicle and a firm irregular intratesticular mass. There is no fever, dysuria or trauma. He asks whether this might be an infection.
ask: Which ONE initial test BEST characterises this concerning lesion?
options: Empirical long-course antibiotics without imaging
Serum PSA as the sole test
Routine urine dipstick alone and discharge
Needle biopsy through the scrotum before imaging
Urgent scrotal ultrasonography
explanations: Infection lacks supporting inflammatory symptoms and should not delay tumour assessment.
PSA is a prostate marker and does not evaluate testicular masses.
Urinalysis alone cannot classify a testicular mass.
Trans-scrotal biopsy is generally avoided for suspected germ-cell malignancy due to scrotal violation concerns.
A solid intratesticular mass is malignant until excluded; urgent scrotal ultrasound characterises the lesion and guides urology review.
pearl: Firm painless intratesticular mass: ultrasound, tumour markers and urgent urology review.
pivot: Acute painful testis with high-riding position and absent cremasteric reflex suggests torsion and should not be delayed by imaging when suspicion is high.

stem: A 51-year-old woman undergoes thyroidectomy. Afterwards she has hoarseness and a weak cough, but her palate is symmetric and shoulder strength intact.
ask: Which ONE nerve is MOST LIKELY injured?
options: Spinal accessory nerve
Recurrent laryngeal nerve
Hypoglossal nerve
Greater auricular nerve
Phrenic nerve
explanations: Accessory nerve injury causes shoulder shrug weakness.
Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury causes ipsilateral vocal fold paresis, producing hoarseness and impaired glottic closure after thyroid surgery.
Hypoglossal injury causes tongue deviation/weakness.
Greater auricular injury causes cutaneous sensory loss near ear/neck.
Phrenic injury impairs diaphragmatic function rather than isolated voice changes.
pearl: External superior laryngeal nerve injury affects pitch control; recurrent laryngeal injury causes vocal fold weakness.
pivot: Stridor or airway compromise after bilateral vocal fold paralysis requires urgent airway assessment.

stem: A 64-year-old smoker has confusion and a serum sodium of 119 mmol/L. He appears euvolaemic. Serum osmolality is low, urine osmolality is 510 mOsm/kg and urine sodium is 55 mmol/L. Thyroid and adrenal function are normal.
ask: Which ONE mechanism BEST explains this biochemical pattern?
options: Appropriate renal suppression of antidiuretic hormone
Primary polydipsia with maximally dilute urine
Osmotic diuresis from severe hyperglycaemia
Inappropriately persistent antidiuretic hormone action
Hypovolaemia-driven sodium conservation by the kidneys
explanations: Suppressed ADH would produce very dilute urine.
Polydipsia usually allows maximally dilute urine.
Osmotic diuresis produces a different biochemical and volume context.
Hypotonic hyponatraemia with concentrated urine, inappropriately high urine sodium and euvolaemia suggests SIADH once endocrine and renal mimics are excluded.
Hypovolaemia commonly produces lower urine sodium unless diuretics or renal salt wasting confound it.
pearl: SIADH is a diagnosis of exclusion; check medications, pulmonary/CNS disease and possible malignancy.
pivot: With seizures from severe hyponatraemia, urgently treat symptoms with carefully controlled hypertonic saline, irrespective of the underlying cause.

stem: A woman in established labour has recurrent late decelerations on CTG, baseline 165/min and variability of 2–3 bpm for over 30 minutes. Oxytocin is running and contractions occur six times in ten minutes.
ask: Which ONE immediate action is MOST APPROPRIATE?
options: Increase oxytocin to shorten labour
Ignore the CTG because late decelerations are normal
Continue unchanged for two hours before notifying anyone
Perform fetal scalp stimulation as the only intervention
Stop oxytocin, correct reversible causes and urgently escalate for possible expedited birth
explanations: More oxytocin worsens uterine hyperstimulation.
Persistent late decelerations are not physiologic reassurance.
Delay prolongs suspected hypoxia.
Scalp stimulation alone does not address ongoing hyperstimulation and possible fetal compromise.
Tachysystole with late decelerations and minimal variability suggests fetal compromise; stop uterotonic stimulation and initiate intrauterine resuscitative measures with senior review.
pearl: Recurrent late decelerations plus reduced variability are more concerning than isolated variable decelerations.
pivot: If tracing rapidly normalises after correcting tachysystole, delivery urgency can be reassessed clinically.

stem: A 68-year-old man arrives with sudden right-sided weakness and aphasia that began 50 minutes ago. His point-of-care glucose is 2.3 mmol/L. He is conscious and can swallow safely.
ask: Which ONE is the MOST APPROPRIATE immediate step?
options: Give intravenous thrombolysis before checking response to glucose
Start therapeutic heparin immediately
Arrange lumbar puncture to exclude meningitis
Discharge because hypoglycaemia excludes stroke
Correct the hypoglycaemia and reassess the neurological deficit
explanations: Thrombolysis decisions require exclusion of mimics and appropriate imaging.
Routine therapeutic anticoagulation is not acute stroke first-line management.
There is no suggestion of meningitis and LP delays time-critical care.
Stroke may coexist, so improvement or further urgent assessment is essential.
Hypoglycaemia is a reversible stroke mimic and must be corrected promptly; persistent focal signs then need an urgent stroke pathway and imaging.
pearl: Always check bedside glucose in a patient with acute focal neurological symptoms.
pivot: If the glucose is normal, proceed directly with urgent stroke assessment and brain imaging without delaying for nonessential tests.

stem: A 54-year-old man is receiving intensive chemotherapy. He develops fever 38.8°C and ANC 0.3 × 10⁹/L. BP 116/74 mmHg; there is no obvious source of infection. Blood cultures have just been taken.
ask: Which ONE is the MOST APPROPRIATE immediate treatment?
options: Administer oral amoxicillin/clavulanate and review tomorrow without formal risk assessment
Wait for a chest X-ray to locate the infection before antibiotics
Give granulocyte-colony stimulating factor as sole immediate treatment
Prompt empirical IV antipseudomonal antibiotics according to local febrile neutropenia protocol
Observe until repeat neutrophils confirm an absolute count below 0.1 × 10⁹/L
explanations: High-risk febrile neutropenia needs immediate IV coverage; outpatient pathways are only for selected low-risk cases after assessment.
Source imaging should not delay empirical antibiotics.
G-CSF is an adjunct in selected cases, not acute antimicrobial coverage.
High-risk febrile neutropenia is a time-critical infection even when clinically stable and source-negative; empirical antibiotics should be given promptly.
ANC 0.3 with fever is already high risk and warrants treatment.
pearl: Neutropenic patients may not form classic pus or inflammatory signs; a seemingly mild fever can be serious.
pivot: Clearly low-risk stable patients may meet criteria for supervised outpatient management after formal risk assessment, not casual observation.

stem: A 35-year-old woman has weight loss, dizziness and recurrent vomiting. She is hypotensive with hyperpigmented palmar creases. Sodium is 125 mmol/L, potassium 5.9 mmol/L, glucose 3.0 mmol/L and early-morning cortisol is very low.
ask: Which ONE diagnosis BEST explains the combination?
options: Syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion alone
Primary adrenal insufficiency with adrenal crisis
Hyperthyroidism without adrenal involvement
Primary hyperaldosteronism
Isolated gastroenteritis causing every abnormality
explanations: SIADH does not typically cause hyperkalaemia or pigmentation.
Hypotension, pigmentation, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and low cortisol strongly support primary adrenal failure; urgent hydrocortisone and isotonic fluids are indicated.
Hyperthyroidism alone does not explain mineralocorticoid deficiency.
Hyperaldosteronism causes hypertension and often low potassium.
Gastroenteritis may precipitate crisis but does not unify chronic pigmentation and mineralocorticoid abnormalities.
pearl: In suspected adrenal crisis, take cortisol/ACTH if immediately feasible but do not delay steroid treatment.
pivot: Secondary adrenal insufficiency often spares aldosterone, making severe hyperkalaemia less typical.

stem: A 2-year-old with several days of viral symptoms has a sudden episode of pallor, lethargy and inconsolable crying. He draws his legs up; episodes recur every 15 minutes. Ultrasound shows a target sign.
ask: Which ONE diagnosis is MOST LIKELY?
options: Pyloric stenosis
Intussusception
Acute appendicitis
Malrotation ruled out by age
Congenital Hirschsprung disease
explanations: Pyloric stenosis typically presents earlier with progressive nonbilious projectile vomiting.
Episodic colicky pain and lethargy with a sonographic target are typical of intestinal intussusception; urgent paediatric surgical/radiology involvement is needed.
Appendicitis more often causes persistent focal pain and is less typical at age two.
Malrotation remains possible at any age but the target sign supports intussusception.
Hirschsprung classically causes delayed meconium/longstanding constipation and distension.
pearl: Currant-jelly stool is a late finding, not required to diagnose intussusception.
pivot: Perforation, shock or peritonitis may require surgery rather than enema reduction.

stem: A 58-year-old man taking NSAIDs for arthritis presents with black tarry stools and lightheadedness. BUN is disproportionately elevated relative to creatinine. His haemoglobin has fallen from 132 to 94 g/L.
ask: Which ONE source is MOST CONSISTENT with this presentation?
options: Simple haemorrhoidal bleeding
Uncomplicated diverticulosis without bleeding
Minor anal fissure
Upper gastrointestinal haemorrhage
Isolated microscopic haematuria
explanations: Haemorrhoids usually cause fresh red rectal blood.
Diverticular bleeding classically causes painless fresh or maroon blood rather than melena.
Fissures cause painful small-volume bright-red blood.
Melena, NSAID risk and increased urea due to absorbed digested blood favour an upper GI bleeding source.
Urinary blood does not produce melena.
pearl: BUN/creatinine disproportion can support an upper GI source but cannot replace resuscitation or endoscopic assessment.
pivot: A brisk upper GI haemorrhage may cause haematochezia rather than melena.

stem: A 47-year-old man has recurrent episodes of sudden intense fear, palpitations, dyspnoea and fear of dying, peaking within minutes. He has subsequently avoided exercise for three months because he fears another episode, and cardiac testing is reassuring.
ask: Which ONE diagnosis is MOST LIKELY?
options: Generalised anxiety disorder as the only diagnosis
Social anxiety disorder
Panic disorder
Specific phobia of animals
Somatic symptom disorder without panic attacks
explanations: GAD causes pervasive excessive worry across multiple domains over time, not discrete unanticipated surges as the defining feature.
Social anxiety centres on scrutiny and social performance.
Recurrent unexpected panic attacks followed by persistent worry or maladaptive avoidance fits panic disorder.
Animal phobia is tied to a specific external trigger.
Somatic symptom disorder focuses on distress around symptoms and does not best explain classic recurrent unexpected panic.
pearl: A panic attack is a symptom; panic disorder requires persistent concern/behavioural change and exclusion of other causes.
pivot: If attacks occur only in public speaking situations, social anxiety with situational panic may be more appropriate.

stem: A pregnant woman at 27 weeks has persistent fever, maternal tachycardia, uterine tenderness and foul-smelling amniotic fluid following prolonged rupture of membranes. Fetal heart rate is 175/min.
ask: Which ONE is the MOST APPROPRIATE management strategy?
options: Tocolysis to maintain pregnancy for another month
Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and prompt delivery planning after stabilisation
Await final cultures before starting antibiotics
Discharge with oral analgesics only
Administer a cervical cerclage
explanations: Tocolysis is generally contraindicated in suspected infection.
Clinical intra-amniotic infection requires prompt antimicrobials and obstetric evaluation for birth; prolonged expectant management can endanger both mother and fetus.
Cultures should not delay antibiotics.
Infection may progress to sepsis.
Cerclage does not treat infection or ruptured membranes.
pearl: Maternal fever, uterine tenderness, fetal tachycardia and purulent fluid suggest chorioamnionitis.
pivot: If membranes are ruptured but there is no evidence of infection or compromise, gestation-specific expectant PPROM protocols may apply.

stem: A 44-year-old woman has sudden severe right upper-quadrant pain, fever and jaundice. She is hypotensive, confused and has a bilirubin of 130 μmol/L. Ultrasound shows a dilated common bile duct.
ask: Which ONE definitive intervention is MOST TIME CRITICAL after resuscitation and antibiotics?
options: Elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy in six months
Urgent biliary decompression, usually by ERCP
Oral ursodeoxycholic acid alone
Observation until bilirubin normalises spontaneously
Routine colonoscopy
explanations: Delayed elective surgery does not drain an infected obstructed duct.
This is severe ascending cholangitis with organ dysfunction from an obstructed infected biliary tree; prompt drainage achieves source control.
Ursodeoxycholic acid is not emergency source control.
Waiting risks septic deterioration.
Colonoscopy does not access the biliary tree.
pearl: Charcot triad plus hypotension/confusion suggests severe cholangitis; treat and drain the obstructed system.
pivot: If the patient only has uncomplicated biliary colic, urgent biliary drainage is generally unnecessary.

stem: A 25-year-old woman has unilateral pelvic pain, spotting and a positive urine pregnancy test. TVUS shows no intrauterine gestational sac and a 2.8-cm adnexal mass. Her BP is 84/50 mmHg and she has shoulder-tip pain.
ask: Which ONE management choice is MOST APPROPRIATE?
options: Urgent operative management for suspected ruptured ectopic pregnancy
Outpatient methotrexate without resuscitation
Repeat urine pregnancy test in two weeks
Reassure her that early pregnancy pain is physiological
Perform endometrial ablation
explanations: Haemodynamic instability with ectopic features and shoulder-tip pain suggests intraperitoneal bleeding; urgent resuscitation and surgery take priority.
Methotrexate is for carefully selected stable, unruptured ectopics.
Follow-up alone is unsafe with shock.
This is a potentially life-threatening diagnosis.
Ablation neither diagnoses nor treats an ectopic pregnancy.
pearl: In ectopic pregnancy, haemodynamic stability determines whether medical or expectant management can be considered.
pivot: A stable patient with appropriately low hCG and small unruptured ectopic may be eligible for supervised nonoperative management.

stem: A 31-year-old G2P1 at 29 weeks has painless fresh vaginal bleeding. Her uterus is soft and non-tender, with a normal fetal heart rate. A low-lying placenta was seen on the 20-week scan.
ask: Which ONE step is MOST IMPORTANT before considering a digital vaginal examination?
options: Perform a digital vaginal examination immediately to estimate dilatation
Give oxytocin to stop bleeding
Assume placental abruption because any third-trimester bleed is painful
Confirm placental location by ultrasound and avoid digital examination until placenta praevia is excluded
Discharge without maternal assessment
explanations: A finger examination can trigger catastrophic bleeding with praevia.
Oxytocin is not an initial treatment for antepartum bleeding due to praevia.
Abruption often causes pain and uterine tenderness, although presentations can vary.
Painless antepartum bleeding with a low-lying placenta suggests placenta praevia; digital examination risks provoking major haemorrhage.
Maternal vitals, fetal monitoring and bleeding assessment remain essential.
pearl: Never perform digital vaginal examination for antepartum bleeding until placenta praevia has been excluded.
pivot: If there is painful bleeding with a tense tender uterus and fetal distress, placental abruption becomes more likely.

stem: A 4-year-old with fever has inspiratory stridor at rest, a barking cough and suprasternal recession. He is alert but distressed and has SpO₂ 94% on air.
ask: Which ONE is the MOST APPROPRIATE immediate pharmacological management?
options: Dexamethasone alone followed by immediate discharge despite resting stridor
Nebulised salbutamol plus oral prednisolone as the only acute treatment
Nebulised adrenaline alone without a corticosteroid
Immediate intubation without trial of appropriate therapy in a currently alert child
Dexamethasone plus nebulised adrenaline with observation and reassessment
explanations: Steroid is essential but significant stridor at rest benefits from nebulised adrenaline and observation.
Salbutamol targets bronchospasm and is less useful in subglottic oedema.
Adrenaline improves symptoms quickly but wears off; steroid treats ongoing inflammation.
Intubation is reserved for deteriorating or failing patients by skilled staff, not automatically all alert croup cases.
Moderate-to-severe croup with stridor at rest responds to corticosteroids and nebulised adrenaline; observe for rebound and escalate if failing.
pearl: Croup = barking cough, hoarseness and inspiratory stridor; keep the child calm.
pivot: Drooling, toxic appearance, tripod positioning or severe dysphagia suggests epiglottitis or bacterial tracheitis rather than simple croup.

stem: A 58-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer has severe back pain and new bilateral leg weakness. He has reduced perianal sensation and difficulty passing urine. His temperature is normal.
ask: Which ONE investigation is MOST URGENT?
options: Routine lumbar X-ray next week
MRI of the whole spine for suspected metastatic spinal cord compression
Bone density scan
Nerve conduction study as the first test
Pelvic ultrasound alone
explanations: Plain radiographs cannot exclude epidural compression.
Cancer, new motor deficit and sphincter/perineal symptoms suggest metastatic cord or cauda equina compression, requiring emergency MRI and specialist escalation.
Bone density is not relevant to acute neurological compromise.
Electrophysiology is too slow and not first-line in suspected compression.
Ultrasound cannot visualise spinal neural structures.
pearl: Back pain plus cancer plus new neurological or bladder symptoms is spinal cord compression until excluded.
pivot: If bacterial infection risks, fever and focal spinal tenderness coexist, spinal epidural abscess is another MRI emergency.

stem: A 72-year-old woman with pneumonia remains hypotensive at 80/45 mmHg after an initial appropriate crystalloid bolus. She is confused, her lactate is 5.1 mmol/L, and the team has already given broad-spectrum antibiotics. There is no evidence of active haemorrhage.
ask: Which ONE is the MOST APPROPRIATE next haemodynamic intervention?
options: Start a titrated noradrenaline infusion while reassessing fluid responsiveness
Give a further fixed 2 L of crystalloid without assessing fluid responsiveness
Start dobutamine as the sole initial vasoactive agent
Begin IV hydrocortisone instead of any vasopressor
Delay vasoactive support until central venous access is placed
explanations: Persistent shock after initial fluid resuscitation requires vasopressor support, usually noradrenaline, with monitored reassessment of perfusion and volume status.
A fixed large fluid dose without reassessment risks overload when initial fluid resuscitation has failed.
Dobutamine is an inotrope used in select low-output states, not the usual first vasopressor for septic vasodilation.
Steroids may help refractory shock but do not replace initial norepinephrine support.
Peripheral vasopressor initiation via a suitable monitored line can be appropriate while central access is arranged; do not prolong shock.
pearl: In septic shock, treat infection and restore perfusion simultaneously; MAP around 65 mmHg is a usual initial target.
pivot: If the patient has massive active bleeding, haemorrhage control and blood products take priority over a sepsis pathway.

stem: A 28-year-old man has initially vague central abdominal pain that localises to the right iliac fossa after ten hours. He now has pain when coughing or walking.
ask: Which ONE explanation BEST accounts for the change in pain localisation?
options: Inflammation spreads from visceral afferents to the somatically innervated parietal peritoneum
The inflamed appendix switches from sympathetic to parasympathetic arterial supply
The ureter starts referring pain to the groin
Pain shifts when the pelvic splanchnic nerves are severed
Somatic pain begins centrally and then becomes visceral pain
explanations: Early appendiceal visceral afferents produce poorly localised periumbilical pain; later parietal peritoneal irritation produces focal somatic pain.
Arterial autonomic supply does not account for the symptom migration.
Ureteric colic usually has flank-to-groin radiation and urinary clues.
No nerve severing is involved.
The actual order is visceral then somatic, not the reverse.
pearl: Pain migration in appendicitis tests neuroanatomy as well as diagnosis.
pivot: A retrocaecal or pelvic appendix may cause atypical pain or signs even with the same underlying process.

stem: A 29-year-old at 35+4 weeks has severe headache, visual flashes and epigastric pain. BP is 174/116 mmHg twice, platelets 80 × 10⁹/L and ALT 150 U/L. The fetal heart rate is presently reassuring.
ask: Which ONE is the MOST APPROPRIATE initial management plan?
options: Discharge on oral analgesia because fetal monitoring is reassuring
Wait until 40 weeks for spontaneous labour
Administer low-dose aspirin alone and review next week
Admit urgently, stabilise BP, give magnesium sulfate and plan delivery after maternal stabilisation
Give diuretics routinely before any other therapy
explanations: Reassuring CTG does not neutralise severe maternal disease.
Expectant term management risks seizure, stroke and organ failure.
Aspirin prevents risk in selected earlier pregnancies but does not treat established severe disease.
Severe pre-eclampsia with possible HELLP requires urgent maternal stabilisation, seizure prophylaxis, antihypertensives and timely birth planning.
Routine diuretics are not initial treatment unless a specific indication such as pulmonary oedema exists.
pearl: Maternal stabilisation precedes delivery where feasible; magnesium prevents/treats eclamptic seizures.
pivot: At earlier gestation with mild disease, specialist expectant surveillance may be considered depending on maternal–fetal condition.

stem: A 23-year-old man sustains a deep laceration just proximal to the volar wrist. He cannot oppose his thumb and has reduced sensation over the palmar tips of the index and middle fingers.
ask: Which ONE nerve has MOST LIKELY been damaged?
options: Median nerve
Ulnar nerve at Guyon canal
Radial nerve in the radial tunnel
Anterior interosseous nerve alone
Recurrent motor branch of the median nerve alone
explanations: Thenar opposition and sensation in lateral digits point to median nerve injury at the wrist.
Ulnar injury primarily affects interossei and ulnar digit sensation, not index fingertip sensation.
Radial dysfunction affects extension and posterior sensory distribution.
AIN injury causes a motor pinch problem but spares cutaneous sensation.
A pure recurrent branch injury weakens thenar muscles but should not affect sensation in the index and middle fingers.
pearl: Carpal tunnel is also median neuropathy but often spares thenar eminence skin sensation due to the palmar cutaneous branch.
pivot: Weak finger abduction with numbness in the little finger instead suggests ulnar injury.

stem: A term newborn becomes cyanosed during feeding on day 2. Preductal saturation in the right hand is 92%, postductal foot saturation is 76%. Femoral pulses are weak, the baby is acidotic and the ductus arteriosus is closing.
ask: Which ONE physiological problem is MOST LIKELY?
options: Isolated small ventricular septal defect
Physiological neonatal jaundice
Duct-dependent systemic blood flow such as critical coarctation of the aorta
Transient tachypnoea alone
Uncomplicated patent foramen ovale
explanations: A small VSD rarely causes neonatal shock from duct closure.
Jaundice does not cause this differential saturation and pulse pattern.
A closing ductus can critically reduce descending aortic perfusion in left-sided obstructive lesions, causing lower-body desaturation, weak femorals and acidosis.
TTN does not typically cause weak femoral pulses and circulatory acidosis.
PFO by itself rarely produces this obstructive shock pattern.
pearl: For suspected duct-dependent circulation, urgently seek neonatal/cardiology help and start prostaglandin E₁ where indicated.
pivot: Duct-dependent pulmonary lesions may present with profound central cyanosis but relatively preserved systemic pulses.

stem: A 67-year-old woman is admitted with atrial fibrillation at 150/min. She is cool and clammy with BP 72/40 mmHg, pulmonary oedema and reduced consciousness. The monitor confirms an irregular narrow-complex tachycardia.
ask: Which ONE is the MOST APPROPRIATE immediate rhythm intervention?
options: Give IV diltiazem for rapid rate control despite profound hypotension
Start an oral beta-blocker and reassess after one hour
Synchronised electrical cardioversion
Commence amiodarone infusion and postpone cardioversion until it finishes
Obtain TOE to exclude atrial thrombus before any rhythm intervention
explanations: Negative inotropy/vasodilation from diltiazem can worsen unstable shock.
Oral therapy is slow and unsafe in pulmonary oedema with reduced consciousness.
Haemodynamic instability directly attributable to rapid atrial fibrillation requires urgent synchronised cardioversion with resuscitation and appropriate sedation where feasible.
Antiarrhythmic infusion should not delay electrical cardioversion in life-threatening instability.
Elective rhythm control often considers atrial thrombus, but immediate haemodynamic rescue cannot wait.
pearl: Unstable tachyarrhythmia: electricity usually takes precedence over routine rate-control drugs.
pivot: In stable AF, rate control, stroke risk assessment and rhythm strategy can be individualised.

stem: A 22-year-old with new-onset mania has not slept for five days, is grandiose and has spent all his savings. He refuses admission, saying he is invincible. He cannot explain the risks of going home or compare alternatives.
ask: Which ONE principle BEST guides capacity assessment for this decision?
options: Assume incapacity from the diagnosis of bipolar disorder alone
Assume capacity solely because he is over 18
Assume incapacity whenever a patient disagrees with a clinician
Ask only whether he can state his full name and address
Assess his ability to understand, retain, use or weigh relevant information, and communicate a choice
explanations: A psychiatric diagnosis by itself does not prove incapacity.
Adult age does not guarantee capacity for every decision.
Unwise choices alone do not establish incapacity.
Orientation is not a substitute for functional decision-making capacity.
Capacity is decision- and time-specific and depends on functional abilities, especially using and weighing information affected by mental illness.
pearl: Decision-making capacity ≠ agreement with doctors; document the actual abilities assessed.
pivot: Even if capacity is present, relevant mental-health legislation may separately govern compulsory assessment when criteria are met.

stem: A 32-year-old patient taking haloperidol develops fever 40°C, severe “lead-pipe” rigidity, altered mental state, autonomic instability and CK 8,000 U/L. Examination shows no inducible clonus.
ask: Which ONE syndrome is MOST LIKELY?
options: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Serotonin syndrome
Acute uncomplicated akathisia
Opioid withdrawal
Anticholinergic toxicity
explanations: Severe rigidity, hyperthermia, autonomic dysfunction and CK rise after dopamine blockade point to NMS.
Serotonin syndrome more characteristically causes hyperreflexia and clonus, often with rapid onset after serotonergic exposure.
Akathisia is restlessness without marked rigidity and systemic organ injury.
Opioid withdrawal produces sympathetic and GI symptoms but not lead-pipe rigidity.
Anticholinergic toxidrome has dry skin and reduced bowel activity, not this classic rigidity pattern.
pearl: NMS = dopamine blockade + rigidity + fever; stop the offending agent and treat urgently.
pivot: If clonus and brisk reflexes dominate after serotonergic drugs, serotonin toxicity moves higher on the differential.

stem: A 38-year-old woman with long-term alcohol dependence stops drinking abruptly. At 36 hours she is tremulous and tachycardic and reports visual hallucinations. She becomes increasingly confused, diaphoretic and hypertensive.
ask: Which ONE management strategy is MOST APPROPRIATE?
options: Haloperidol monotherapy with no withdrawal treatment
Inpatient monitored benzodiazepine-based alcohol withdrawal treatment with thiamine and supportive care
Discharge with reassurance that confusion is expected
Administer disulfiram during the acute episode
Treat only with oral propranolol
explanations: Antipsychotic monotherapy does not prevent withdrawal seizures and may lower seizure threshold.
Delirium with autonomic instability after cessation of alcohol suggests severe withdrawal, requiring monitored sedative treatment, thiamine and complication surveillance.
Withdrawal delirium is potentially fatal.
Disulfiram is not treatment for acute withdrawal.
Beta-blockade masks adrenergic signs without treating the underlying withdrawal risk.
pearl: Use thiamine in patients at risk of deficiency; evaluate glucose and electrolytes and avoid undertreating withdrawal.
pivot: If hallucinations occur without delirium or severe autonomic disturbance, alcohol-induced hallucinosis may be considered but still warrants assessment.

stem: A 25-year-old with bipolar disorder has taken lithium for three years. After gastroenteritis and dehydration, she develops coarse tremor, ataxia, vomiting and slurred speech. Her creatinine is elevated.
ask: Which ONE diagnosis BEST explains the new symptoms?
options: Serotonin syndrome due to lithium alone without a serotonergic combination
A normal benign fine lithium tremor
Lithium toxicity precipitated by dehydration and reduced renal clearance
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome without dopamine blockade
Acute extrapyramidal dystonia
explanations: Serotonin syndrome usually includes hyperreflexia/clonus in a serotonergic context.
A benign lithium tremor is usually fine and lacks ataxia or systemic illness.
Coarse tremor, cerebellar dysfunction and GI symptoms during renal impairment are typical of lithium accumulation.
NMS is associated with dopamine blockade, rigidity and marked autonomic disturbance.
Acute dystonia causes sustained abnormal postures rather than ataxia.
pearl: Lithium is renally cleared; dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and some diuretics can raise concentrations.
pivot: If symptoms are severe, obtain urgent toxicology/renal input and assess the need for extracorporeal removal; do not rely on the level alone.

stem: A 67-year-old woman develops sudden severe pain in one eye with blurred vision, halos around lights, headache and vomiting. The cornea is hazy, pupil is mid-dilated and intraocular pressure is markedly elevated.
ask: Which ONE diagnosis and management priority is MOST APPROPRIATE?
options: Uncomplicated conjunctivitis managed with lubricants only
Posterior vitreous detachment with routine follow-up
Migraine aura requiring only analgesia
Acute angle-closure glaucoma requiring immediate pressure-lowering treatment and ophthalmology
Chronic open-angle glaucoma with no urgency
explanations: Conjunctivitis does not cause dramatic pressure elevation or a mid-dilated pupil.
PVD usually causes flashes/floaters without severe ocular pain.
Migraine does not explain high eye pressure and corneal oedema.
Severe painful red eye, cloudy cornea, fixed mid-dilated pupil and high pressure are classic acute angle closure, an eye emergency.
Chronic open-angle glaucoma typically progresses silently.
pearl: A painful red eye with reduced vision is never routine conjunctivitis until serious causes are excluded.
pivot: If painless flashes, floaters and a curtain-like visual field defect predominate, urgently exclude retinal detachment.

stem: A 3-week-old infant is brought in with poor feeding, lethargy and a temperature of 38.4°C. There are no focal findings and the infant briefly appears more alert after a feed.
ask: Which ONE approach is MOST APPROPRIATE?
options: Reassure because the infant improved after feeding
Prescribe oral antihistamine for presumed viral illness
Delay all investigations until fever persists for seven days
Urgent hospital assessment for serious bacterial infection with cultures and empiric IV antibiotics
Arrange routine vaccination as the only intervention
explanations: Transient improvement does not exclude neonatal sepsis.
Antihistamines have no role in a febrile neonate.
Waiting risks rapid deterioration.
Fever at 3 weeks is high risk for invasive bacterial infection even without focal signs; prompt evaluation and parenteral antibiotics are indicated.
Vaccination is unrelated to management of this emergency.
pearl: A febrile neonate can look deceptively well; age changes the threshold for sepsis evaluation.
pivot: In an older fully immunised child who looks well, risk-stratified assessment differs according to age and findings.

stem: A 42-year-old woman has fatigue, constipation, galactorrhoea and menstrual irregularity. Blood tests show very high TSH, low free T4 and mildly raised prolactin. There is no visual-field deficit.
ask: Which ONE explanation is MOST LIKELY for the raised prolactin?
options: Increased TRH drive secondary to primary hypothyroidism
A prolactinoma is certain regardless of the thyroid results
Hyperthyroidism-driven dopamine excess
Excess adrenal aldosterone secretion
An ovarian torsion
explanations: Primary hypothyroidism raises hypothalamic TRH, which stimulates both TSH and prolactin release.
Prolactinoma is possible but not the most parsimonious explanation without treating hypothyroidism.
Hyperthyroidism would usually suppress TSH.
Aldosterone does not explain this axis.
Ovarian torsion presents acutely with pelvic pain.
pearl: Check thyroid function in hyperprolactinaemia; treating hypothyroidism can normalise prolactin.
pivot: If prolactin remains markedly elevated after correction or there are visual symptoms, pituitary evaluation is indicated.

stem: A 29-year-old contact lens wearer has a painful photophobic red eye, reduced vision and a white corneal infiltrate. Fluorescein shows an epithelial defect overlying the opacity.
ask: Which ONE condition is MOST CONCERNING?
options: Uncomplicated allergic conjunctivitis
Painless subconjunctival haemorrhage
Microbial keratitis with corneal ulceration
Presbyopia
Isolated refractive error
explanations: Allergy causes itching and watery discharge, not a focal ulcer with visual reduction.
Subconjunctival haemorrhage is usually painless with preserved vision.
Contact lenses plus marked pain, photophobia and a corneal infiltrate/ulcer suggest microbial keratitis, which can rapidly threaten sight.
Presbyopia causes gradual near-vision difficulties.
Refractive error does not inflame or ulcerate the cornea.
pearl: Contact lens wearers with a painful red eye and vision change need same-day urgent ophthalmic assessment.
pivot: If there is a dendritic fluorescein lesion, herpes simplex keratitis becomes a key alternative.

stem: A 56-year-old man has severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and serum lipase six times the upper limit of normal. His ALT is markedly elevated and ultrasound shows gallstones but no visible common bile duct stone. He has no fever or jaundice.
ask: Which ONE is the MOST APPROPRIATE approach to biliary intervention?
options: Perform urgent ERCP for every case of gallstone pancreatitis
Perform immediate laparoscopic cholecystectomy before treating acute pancreatitis in all cases
Give prophylactic IV antibiotics to prevent pancreatic necrosis
Obtain a routine MRCP and ERCP in every gallstone-pancreatitis patient regardless of obstruction
Reserve urgent ERCP for evidence of cholangitis or ongoing biliary obstruction
explanations: ERCP without cholangitis/obstruction offers limited benefit and has harms.
Cholecystectomy is important, often during the same admission for mild disease, but its exact timing depends on acute severity.
Antibiotics are not routinely given for sterile pancreatitis.
Duct imaging may help uncertain obstruction; automatically doing both is unwarranted.
Gallstone pancreatitis usually needs supportive care and definitive gallbladder management; ERCP is urgent when cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction is suspected.
pearl: Distinguish gallstone pancreatitis from cholangitis: fever, jaundice, sepsis and obstructive features change urgency.
pivot: If jaundice and ascending cholangitis develop, prompt biliary drainage becomes essential.

stem: A 26-year-old woman becomes acutely breathless and hypotensive shortly after delivering her baby. She has diffuse oozing from venepuncture sites and a sudden fall in oxygen saturation. A bedside echocardiogram shows acute right ventricular strain.
ask: Which ONE is the MOST LIKELY underlying obstetric emergency?
options: Postpartum endometritis
Anaphylaxis limited to a skin reaction
Peripartum cardiomyopathy alone
Amniotic fluid embolism
Aspiration pneumonitis with no other complication
explanations: Endometritis develops over hours to days with fever and uterine tenderness.
Anaphylaxis can cause collapse but usually has an exposure trigger and does not classically produce immediate DIC.
Cardiomyopathy causes heart failure but not typically sudden consumptive coagulopathy.
Abrupt cardiorespiratory collapse during or soon after birth combined with disseminated coagulopathy is characteristic of amniotic fluid embolism, a clinical diagnosis.
Aspiration causes hypoxia but does not explain immediate systemic bleeding and RV strain as well.
pearl: Classic amniotic fluid embolism: sudden hypoxia, hypotension and coagulopathy; provide critical care support immediately.
pivot: Without coagulopathy, consider other causes of peripartum collapse such as pulmonary thromboembolism, anaphylaxis or haemorrhage.

stem: A 76-year-old woman falls onto an outstretched hand. X-ray shows a displaced distal radius fracture with dorsal angulation and displacement of the distal fragment.
ask: Which ONE eponymous fracture pattern is described?
options: Smith fracture
Bennett fracture
Scaphoid waist fracture
Colles fracture
Monteggia fracture-dislocation
explanations: Smith fracture has volar displacement/angulation and is often described as reverse Colles.
Bennett involves the base of the first metacarpal.
Scaphoid fracture involves carpal bone tenderness in the snuffbox.
A Colles fracture is a dorsally angulated/displaced distal radius fracture, classically from a FOOSH mechanism.
Monteggia involves ulna fracture with radial head dislocation.
pearl: Colles = dorsal; Smith = volar. Always check neurovascular status and median nerve function.
